catalog_quote: 2.3. Syllable Structure The phonological word in Mnar consists of monosyllabic, sesquisyllabic and multisyllabic roots. Disyllabic words are most frequent and phonologically they are merely the composite of two syllables, each of which follows the same phonological requisites. Trisyllabic words are rare, if found to prevail they are an outcome of word formation (compounding). ... 2.3.2. Sesquisyllabic Structure A distinct syllable type termed ‘sesquisyllabic’ (Matisoff 1973:86) is found to exist in many AA languages (Jenny et al. 2014) wherein a disyllabic word consists of an initial unstressed syllable often called a minor (Henderson 1952) or presyllable followed by a stressed full syllable (main syllable). In this minor or presyllable the nucleus of the syllable is occupied by either of these sonorants (l,r,m,n, ŋ), in lieu of certain weak vowels and as such they carry the main weight…
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Since most AA languages are sesquisyllabic, they tend to be strongly iambic, wherein a weak and unstressed syllable is followed by a strong and full stressed syllable (Jenny et al., 2014). Likewise, the stress in Mnar is generally on the last syllable of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable; in sesquisyllabic (minor + major syllable) words the presyllable (nucleus a syllabic sonorant or reduced vowel) is unstressed and the full final syllable carries stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; hedged only by 'generally'. Di-/trisyllabic words said to arise mostly by affixation/compounding.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on elicited wordlist/sentence data (NEHU MA field report, Jirang village); no phrase-level discussion. NOTE the variety: Mnar of Jirang (Ri Bhoi district), which Glottolog's bibliography codes as War-Jaintia [aml] but whose affiliation is disputed (see identity_note). For War proper (Amwi) the only opened sources are indirect: Daladier 2011:176 says Pnar/War/Lyngngam, unlike Standard Khasi, retain word accentuation (position not stated); Sidwell 2014:151-152 characterizes Khasian words as monosyllables or iambic disyllables, citing Weidert 1975:21 for Amwi word structure.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Mnar (Mynnar), spoken at Jirang, Ri Bhoi district — geographically detached from the War area in the south. Glottolog's bibliography codes Rymbai 2018 as 'Mnar = Mynnar = War-Jaintia [aml]' (hence its listing under warj1242), and Rymbai reports Gurdon (1914) affiliating Mnar with Synteng, Lakadong and Amwi; but Daladier (2011, JSEALS 4.2:176) states Mnar 'turns out to be a Jowai dialect of Pnar' (pnar1238), while also noting an Amwi (War) group settled at Jirang. Treat the attribution to warj1242 as provisional. Glottolog warj1242 comprises Nuclear War-Jaintia [nucl1292] (Amwi, Nongtalang etc.) and War-Khasi [wark1246] (Shella, Lamin, Sohkha, Nongjri); the NEHU theses examined cover both sub-varieties but are silent on stress. The definitive first-hand statement for War proper is expected in Weidert 1975 (Amwi, nucl1292).
